trial.ground_truth: Inventory executes pg_sleep(1.2) before catalog SQL
trial.predicted_root_cause: Live PostgreSQL sessions owned by application_name=inventory-service are executing SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event_type=Timeout / wait_event=PgSleep, and pg_stat_statements reports a pg_sleep statement with mean_exec_time ~1201.96ms (424 calls) plus a second at ~2001.71ms (344 calls). This deliberate 1.2s DB stall inside the inventory product-read path matches the observed ~1206ms inventory-service /products latency, which propagates through order-service /checkout (~1228ms) up to gateway (~1242ms). Latency is essentially constant (p50≈p95, tight spread) with 0% errors, indicating a fixed sleep rather than queueing/contention. The elevated inventory pool counters (requests_queued=491, requests_wait_ms=294317, requests_errors=248) are downstream consequences of holding connections during the sleep, not an independent pool-exhaustion defect. The fault is injected at runtime (runtime.fault() reads 'fault:<name>' keys from Redis), i.e. infrastructure/experiment-level, and is not caused by any logic in the allowlisted pricing.py, which contains only arithmetic.
trial.source: Measured provider usage; unknown values are not estimates
trial.duration_scope: full workflow including recovery waits and Critic

regression_risks: Recommended statement_timeout / query-timeout mitigation could truncate legitimate long-running product queries or prematurely abort pg_sleep-adjacent paths if applied unconditionally.
If Redis fault keys are removed but the underlying harness re-injects, latency can silently return with no code change to detect it.
Untouched pool sizing (max_size=4 in runtime.py line 24) means any real slow query will again hold connections and rebuild the observed queued/error counters.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Evidence is observational, not an interventional test: no controlled removal/re-add of the suspect pg_sleep was tied to a latency delta. Before/after windows are only ~20s each and after-data shows recovery (2.50ms inventory), consistent with operator-run restoration, but the causality_limit explicitly states this does not prove a unique mechanism. No repeat/replication and no Redis key inspection were performed.
critic_result.verification_summary: Core causal chain is well supported: active pg_stat_activity shows application_name=inventory-service running SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) under wait_event_type=Timeout/PgSleep (E-4fb4e47ae3e04ffa, E-33a2f207d8f8413e, E-f0988dcd286e4dec), pg_stat_statements reports two pg_sleep statements with mean_exec_time ~1202ms and ~2002ms (E-f0988dcd286e4dec), and trace E-0224a815dbdd47d5 directly links inventory /products to order-service /checkout and gateway with the ~1206/1228/1242ms constant spread, 0% errors. Latency being p50≈p95 with no errors is consistent with a fixed sleep, not queueing. However, several sub-claims are overstated or unproven: (1) the "injected via Redis fault: keys" mechanism is asserted from code intent (E-cab06d6b47944a91) but never observed; Redis snapshots (E-6ab15fd8523c4cea, E-d64ca85d387a4a5c, E-0c65e5ee8f3b43a4, E-fa80f03919a04788) are cumulative and only show aggregate keyspace totals, no fault key. (2) Pool counters (requests_queued=491, requests_wait_ms=294317, requests_errors=248) are flat across before/after while usage_ms rose only ~7k, so labelling them "downstream consequences of the sleep" is inferential, not demonstrated. (3) The 2.0s pg_sleep variant's role is unexplained. Diagnosis direction (DB stall in inventory product-read path) is sound; precise mechanism and attribution of pool stats remain partially unverified. No production deployment claimed; patch_decision=NO_CODE_PATCH and recovery was operator-run, so this does not assert service restoration by an AI patch.
alternative_explanations: Fixed pg_sleep latency could be produced by a deploy/config-level slow-query shim or a proxy/pool layer delay rather than the unobserved Redis 'fault:' key toggling asserted by the diagnosis.

inventory pool exhaustion/contention (queued=491, errors=248) may be the primary driver of the observed constant latency, with pg_sleep a symptom — the flat counters across the before/after windows weaken the diagnosis's causal direction.
External throttling or a fixed-latency network/load-balancer injection at the gateway->inventory hop could reproduce the constant ~1206ms without DB-side pg_sleep being the sole cause.

The affected service (inventory-service) and the causal mechanism (fixed 1.2s DB sleep, not pool exhaustion/contention) match the ground truth. Higher-level mechanism is accurate; the 2.0s pg_sleep variant and injection-implementation detail are not required to match.

diagnosis.root_cause: Live PostgreSQL sessions owned by application_name=inventory-service are executing SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) with wait_event_type=Timeout / wait_event=PgSleep, and pg_stat_statements reports a pg_sleep statement with mean_exec_time ~1201.96ms (424 calls) plus a second at ~2001.71ms (344 calls). This deliberate 1.2s DB stall inside the inventory product-read path matches the observed ~1206ms inventory-service /products latency, which propagates through order-service /checkout (~1228ms) up to gateway (~1242ms). Latency is essentially constant (p50≈p95, tight spread) with 0% errors, indicating a fixed sleep rather than queueing/contention. The elevated inventory pool counters (requests_queued=491, requests_wait_ms=294317, requests_errors=248) are downstream consequences of holding connections during the sleep, not an independent pool-exhaustion defect. The fault is injected at runtime (runtime.fault() reads 'fault:<name>' keys from Redis), i.e. infrastructure/experiment-level, and is not caused by any logic in the allowlisted pricing.py, which contains only arithmetic.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: Operational only: treat as an injected DB-latency fault. Investigate/remove the runtime fault injection (Redis 'fault:' keys toggled on inventory-service) that appends SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) to the product-read query. If this is an experiment, stop/revert the experiment; if it mirrors a real slow query, add a query timeout / statement_timeout and an index/plan review so a single slow statement cannot hold pool connections. Do not patch pricing.py.

Tight p50/p95 spread with 0% errors rules out pool exhaustion or contention as the primary cause; pool counters are consequences. pricing.py (lines 1-6) contains only price arithmetic and cannot cause the delay, so no code patch in the allowlisted scope is appropriate.
remaining_uncertainty: Exact injection mechanism (harness/config) is inaccessible, so I cannot name the precise code that adds pg_sleep beyond runtime.fault() reading 'fault:' Redis keys.
Whether the 2.0s pg_sleep variant is a separate fault or a compounded path is unconfirmed.

1: import os
2: import json
3: import logging
4: import time
5: from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
6: from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
7: from fastapi.responses import Response
8: from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool
9: from psycopg.rows import dict_row
10: from redis.asyncio import Redis
11: from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, generate_latest, CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST
12: from opentelemetry import trace
13: from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
14: from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
15: from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor
16: from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.http.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter
17: from opentelemetry.instrumentation.fastapi import FastAPIInstrumentor
18: from opentelemetry.instrumentation.httpx import HTTPXClientInstrumentor
19: from opentelemetry.instrumentation.psycopg import PsycopgInstrumentor
20: from opentelemetry.instrumentation.redis import RedisInstrumentor
21: 
22: SERVICE = os.getenv('SERVICE_NAME', 'sentinel')
23: DSN = os.environ['DATABASE_URL']
24: pool = AsyncConnectionPool(DSN, min_size=1, max_size=4, timeout=0.8, open=False, kwargs={'autocommit': True, 'row_factory': dict_row, 'application_name': SERVICE})
25: audit_pool = AsyncConnectionPool(DSN, min_size=1, max_size=2, open=False, kwargs={'autocommit': True})
26: redis = Redis.from_url(os.environ['REDIS_URL'], decode_responses=True)
27: requests = Counter('commerce_requests_total', 'Completed HTTP requests', ['service','path','status'])
28: latency = Histogram('commerce_request_seconds', 'HTTP wall time', ['service','path'], buckets=(.01,.05,.1,.25,.5,1,2,5,10,30))
29: db_queries = Counter('commerce_db_queries_total', 'Business database statements', ['service'])
30: log = logging.getLogger(SERVICE)
31: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
32: 
33: async def query(sql, args=(), one=False):
34:     db_queries.labels(SERVICE).inc()
35:     async with pool.connection() as conn:
36:         cur = await conn.execute(sql, args)
37:         if cur.description:
38:             return await cur.fetchone() if one else await cur.fetchall()
39: 
40: async def fault(name):
41:     return bool(await redis.exists('fault:' + name))
42: 
43: def instrument(app):
44:     provider = TracerProvider(resource=Resource.create({'service.name': SERVICE}))
45:     provider.add_span_processor(BatchSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter(endpoint=os.environ['OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT']+'/v1/traces')))
46:     trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
47:     HTTPXClientInstrumentor().instrument()
48:     PsycopgInstrumentor().instrument()
49:     RedisInstrumentor().instrument()
50:     FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app, excluded_urls='health,metrics')
51: 
52:     @app.middleware('http')
53:     async def record(request: Request, call_next):
54:         if request.url.path in ('/health','/metrics'):
55:             return await call_next(request)
56:         start = time.perf_counter()
57:         status, error = 500, None
58:         tid = format(trace.get_current_span().get_span_context().trace_id, '032x')
59:         try:
60:             response = await call_next(request)
61:             status = response.status_code
62:             response.headers['X-Trace-ID'] = tid
63:             return response
64:         except Exception as exc:
65:             error = f'{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}'
66:             log.exception('request failed')
67:             from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
68:             return JSONResponse({'error': error, 'trace_id': tid}, status_code=500)
69:         finally:
70:             duration = time.perf_counter()-start
71:             path = request.scope.get('route')
72:             path = getattr(path, 'path', request.url.path)
73:             requests.labels(SERVICE,path,str(status)).inc()
74:             latency.labels(SERVICE,path).observe(duration)
75:             event = dict(service=SERVICE,path=path,status=status,duration_ms=round(duration*1000,2),trace_id=tid,error=error)
76:             log.info(json.dumps(event))
77:             try:
78:                 async with audit_pool.connection() as conn:
79:                     await conn.execute('INSERT INTO request_logs(service,path,status,duration_ms,trace_id,error) VALUES(%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)', tuple(event.values()))
80:             except Exception:
81:                 log.exception('audit persistence failed')
82: 
83:     @app.get('/metrics')
84:     async def metrics():
85:         return Response(generate_latest(), media_type=CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST)
86: 
87:     @app.get('/health')
88:     async def health():
89:         await query('SELECT 1')
90:         await redis.ping()
91:         return {'service':SERVICE,'status':'healthy'}
92: 
93:     @app.get('/pool-stats')
94:     async def pool_stats():
95:         return {'service':SERVICE,'source':'Measured','pool':pool.get_stats()}

regression_risks: Recommended statement_timeout / query-timeout mitigation could truncate legitimate long-running product queries or prematurely abort pg_sleep-adjacent paths if applied unconditionally.
If Redis fault keys are removed but the underlying harness re-injects, latency can silently return with no code change to detect it.
Untouched pool sizing (max_size=4 in runtime.py line 24) means any real slow query will again hold connections and rebuild the observed queued/error counters.
critic.test_sufficiency: Evidence is observational, not an interventional test: no controlled removal/re-add of the suspect pg_sleep was tied to a latency delta. Before/after windows are only ~20s each and after-data shows recovery (2.50ms inventory), consistent with operator-run restoration, but the causality_limit explicitly states this does not prove a unique mechanism. No repeat/replication and no Redis key inspection were performed.
critic.verification_summary: Core causal chain is well supported: active pg_stat_activity shows application_name=inventory-service running SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) under wait_event_type=Timeout/PgSleep (E-4fb4e47ae3e04ffa, E-33a2f207d8f8413e, E-f0988dcd286e4dec), pg_stat_statements reports two pg_sleep statements with mean_exec_time ~1202ms and ~2002ms (E-f0988dcd286e4dec), and trace E-0224a815dbdd47d5 directly links inventory /products to order-service /checkout and gateway with the ~1206/1228/1242ms constant spread, 0% errors. Latency being p50≈p95 with no errors is consistent with a fixed sleep, not queueing. However, several sub-claims are overstated or unproven: (1) the "injected via Redis fault: keys" mechanism is asserted from code intent (E-cab06d6b47944a91) but never observed; Redis snapshots (E-6ab15fd8523c4cea, E-d64ca85d387a4a5c, E-0c65e5ee8f3b43a4, E-fa80f03919a04788) are cumulative and only show aggregate keyspace totals, no fault key. (2) Pool counters (requests_queued=491, requests_wait_ms=294317, requests_errors=248) are flat across before/after while usage_ms rose only ~7k, so labelling them "downstream consequences of the sleep" is inferential, not demonstrated. (3) The 2.0s pg_sleep variant's role is unexplained. Diagnosis direction (DB stall in inventory product-read path) is sound; precise mechanism and attribution of pool stats remain partially unverified. No production deployment claimed; patch_decision=NO_CODE_PATCH and recovery was operator-run, so this does not assert service restoration by an AI patch.
alternative_explanations: Fixed pg_sleep latency could be produced by a deploy/config-level slow-query shim or a proxy/pool layer delay rather than the unobserved Redis 'fault:' key toggling asserted by the diagnosis.

inventory pool exhaustion/contention (queued=491, errors=248) may be the primary driver of the observed constant latency, with pg_sleep a symptom — the flat counters across the before/after windows weaken the diagnosis's causal direction.
External throttling or a fixed-latency network/load-balancer injection at the gateway->inventory hop could reproduce the constant ~1206ms without DB-side pg_sleep being the sole cause.
